rows.title: Color
rows.text: You have no eyes, yet light still changes what you do. If you are a dog vomit slime mold, you cannot form your fruiting bodies without light, and in Physarum polycephalum a phytochrome, a light-sensing molecule, is one receptor for the light that makes the slime break into pieces. For most other slime molds, nobody has measured whether you sense light or which colors of it count.
rows.note: R3 (Didymium iridis, light needed for sporulation) left out to keep the row short; it is grade g and could be added.

rows.title: Hunger
rows.text: Picture a plasmodium that has eaten everything around it and is running out of food. In two slime molds, Physarum polycephalum and Didymium iridis, starvation and light are both needed to trigger spore-making, and a review states that the dog vomit slime mold cannot fruit without light. Nobody has measured this in other slime molds, so if you are another species, nobody knows whether you need light to fruit.
rows.note: Left out the year of the review, since no record quote states it. R1 (phytochrome in Physarum) concerns plasmodium fragmentation, not hunger, so I left it out.

rows.title: Food
rows.text: In a two-chamber test, a slime mold called Physarum polycephalum was attracted by glucose, galactose, phosphates and ATP, and repelled by sucrose, fructose and some mineral salts. Nobody has measured which chemicals attract or repel you.
rows.note: Only one species (Physarum polycephalum) has a record; chemical carry across species is not allowed, so the row stays at i.

the number 1938 is in none of the cited records
failed.last: You have no eyes, yet light matters to you, and nobody has measured how most slime molds sense it. If you are a dog vomit slime mold, a 1950 paper reviewing work from 1938 states that you cannot form fruiting bodies without light. If you are Physarum polycephalum, a light-sensing pigment called a phytochrome is one reason your plasmodium breaks into fragments in light, and if you are Didymium iridis, you need both starvation and light before you make spores.

failed.last: If you are a dog vomit slime mold, a 1950 review of earlier work says your plasmodium cannot fruit without light. In another slime mold, Physarum polycephalum, a light-sensing molecule called a phytochrome is one of the receptors that breaks the plasmodium into pieces in light. Nobody has measured how fast you respond to light.
